summary: Weekly POC sync reviewing INT8 vs FP8 quantization runs. FP8 shows higher throughput and lower latency in our tests but has slightly larger quality regressions on a subset of prompts (math/code). Team agreed to run mixed-precision sweeps and a dedicated hardware throughput run. Redwood will share raw benchmarks and security docs. Next check-in after dedicated run scheduling.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-15 / 15:00 UTC / 55m. Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Anya Singh (Redwood Inference Eng) - Daniel Cho (FinSight ML), Priya Nair (FinSight DS), Omar Al-Hassan (FinSight Platform), Kelly (PM).

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: we want to go over the latest quantization runs - INT8 baseline vs FP8 experiments - look at quality deltas, throughput/latency, and agree next steps. Marco and Anya will run through the results.

[00:18] Marco: Cool, I'll start. Quick caveat: these numbers are from our hosted testbed on g5-like hardware emulation; we also have the dedicated run queued up but not executed yet. The test harness is the same one we shared last week, there's a link in the chat to the spreadsheet.

[00:35] Marco: For the model variant you all ran - 13b dense-ish - INT8 quant gave about 1.6x token throughput vs FP32 baseline, median p99 latency down ~20%. FP8 experiments show roughly 2.0x to 2.2x throughput and p99 down ~30%. So raw perf favors FP8.

[00:52] Priya: Wait, is that end-to-end latency including our prefix cache? We noticed caching behavior changes a bit with quantization.

[00:58] Anya: Good question. These numbers include our prefix caching enabled but we had to disable KV-cache warmup optimizations for the FP8 baseline because the low-level kernels are still in a slightly different code path. So the FP8 perf here is with naive KV warmup; on dedicated runtime with optimized kernel selection we expect numbers to shift.

[01:20] Daniel: How about quality? Throughput is great but we can't lose accuracy on business-critical prompts - e.g., numeric extraction and financial Q/A.

[01:25] Marco: Right. We ran your 1k prompt eval set (the one labeled finance-qna-v2) across FP32, INT8, FP8. Metrics: accuracy (exact-match style) for the set: FP32 92.1%, INT8 90.8% (so ~1.3 pt drop), FP8 88.6% (~3.5 pt drop). We also computed ROUGE-L-esque overlaps and saw similar relative regressions.

[01:47] Priya: Hmm FP8 seems to drop more on math/code-oriented prompts, right?

[01:51] Anya: Yes. When we slice the eval by prompt type: for free-form generative text, FP8 is almost indistinguishable. For structured numeric outputs and code-ish answers, FP8 sometimes introduces token substitutions or truncated completions. We suspect a combination of reduced mantissa precision and activation distribution shifts in certain attention layers.

[02:10] Omar: Is there an easy mitigation? Like per-layer mixed precision or preserving key layers in higher precision?

[02:15] Marco: Exactly. We ran a quick sweep where we kept the final two transformer blocks at FP16 while quantizing earlier layers to FP8. That reduced the accuracy gap significantly: FP8-mixed had 90.5% vs FP32 92.1% (so only ~1.6 pt drop) while retaining most of the FP8 throughput gains (~1.9x). We'll share the exact config.

[02:39] Kelly: That sounds promising. What's the engineering complexity on your side to enable mixed precision per-layer in our Dedicated environment?

[02:46] Anya: On Redwood Dedicated it is supported - the runtime supports per-layer dtype overrides and kernel selection. It requires a model quantization config file plus a short restart of the model instance. No code changes on your app. For Private deployments there's the same knob, but on-prem teams may need to accept the new kernel binaries if they restrict package updates.

[03:07] Daniel: Any random regressions we should watch for? We saw one example where a numeric table got munged - like rounding errors displayed as weird tokens.

[03:14] Marco: Yep. We saw two classes: 1) small numeric perturbations in high-precision decimals, 2) occasional copy/paste-like repetition in long code blocks when attention logits had slightly different scaling. Both are fixable with targeted layer FP16 preservation or a micro-calibration pass where we recalibrate output logits on a small set.

[03:37] Priya: How about memory usage? We care about batch sizes for embedding pipelines.

[03:41] Anya: INT8 reduces memory footprint vs FP16 by about 1.8x in our tests; FP8 reduces further - so you can run bigger batches or fewer GPUs. That said, INT8 quant has more mature streaming/batching integration today; FP8 kernels are newer and we had to disable a micro-batching optimization in this run which cost a little throughput. On dedicated optimized kernels we expect FP8 to be even better.

[04:06] Lena: Let's ground this with the customer's target SLOs. Kelly, remind us the P99 latency SLO you're aiming for and cost targets.

[04:14] Kelly: For our product pipeline we want p95 < 250ms and p99 < 600ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens) with cost target of at least 30% reduction vs our current self-hosted baseline. If we can hit that with INT8 that's fine, FP8 would be great if quality holds.

[04:32] Marco: On the hosted testbed INT8 hits p95 ~210ms, p99 ~480ms for 512-token baseline at batch size 4. FP8 was p95 ~170ms, p99 ~420ms, but again that was with a non-optimized KV warmup path. Throughput-wise FP8 is better which helps cost; if quality is acceptable, FP8 mixed precision seems like the sweet spot.

[04:56] Daniel: Can you re-run the 1k eval with the FP8-mixed config? The ~1.6pt drop is borderline for us. If mixed gets within 1pt maybe acceptable.

[05:04] Anya: Yes we can. We'll run FP8-mixed + a few more sweeps: keep last 2 blocks FP16, keep LN scale in FP16, and a variant with only last block FP16. We'll push those CSVs to the shared sheet.

[05:17] Priya: Also please include per-prompt deltas in the sheet - we want to triage which prompts fail.

[05:22] Marco: We'll include per-prompt pass/fail tags and a small 'explain' column where the SE team annotates possible failure modes.

[05:29] Omar: On the infra side, for Dedicated we need to run a dedicated hardware throughput test. Can Redwood schedule capacity?

[05:34] Lena: Yes, Marco will reserve. Marco: can you set a slot week of 7/28? We want g5x- and a37-equivalent runs; also test under two concurrent tenants.

[05:43] Marco: I'll set up reserved runs and send calendar invites. We'll also capture flame graphs and kernel-level counters so we can tune batching and kernel choices.

[05:51] Kelly: Regarding security/compliance - we need SOC2 docs and the KMS/HSM details for Private.

[05:57] Lena: We'll share the SOC2 summary and the KMS integration guide. I'll drop links in the CRM ticket.

[06:03] Daniel: One operational question: if we pick FP8-mixed for production, what's rollback like? Can we quickly fall back to INT8 or FP16?

[06:10] Anya: Yes. Redwood runtime supports pinning model variant + quant config. Rollback is a config switch and a quick instance restart; typical RTO is minutes not hours. We also support A/B/Canary rollouts by route.

[06:23] Priya: Any licensing or binary concerns for on-prem?

[06:26] Marco: For Private, the FP8 kernels are included in our later runtime builds. If you're in an air-gapped environment and freeze binaries, you'd need to accept the kernel update. We'll note that for the security packet.

[06:36] Kelly: Good. Let's talk experimental plan and owners.

[06:39] Lena: Action items - we'll enumerate in the CRM entry. To recap: Redwood shares full CSVs and scripts by 7/17; FinSight runs mixed-precision sweep and returns per-prompt triage by 7/22; Redwood schedules dedicated runs week of 7/28 and shares invites. Security docs 7/18. Next sync after dedicated run scheduling or earlier if we have decisive results.

[07:01] Daniel: Sounds good. One more ask: can you add a short checklist for model selection - e.g., if FP8 drop is >2.5pt on structured prompts, recommend INT8 or mixed?

[07:09] Marco: Yes we'll include a one-pager decision matrix with thresholds and recommended mitigations.

[07:15] Lena: Anything else?

[07:17] Priya: No, thanks. Appreciate the clarity.

[07:20] Lena: Great - thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the CRM and sheet.

[07:25] Meeting end.

Notes: transcript contains minor mis-transcriptions (e.g., kernel names like a37 vs a4x, 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K-V cash', attendee names occasionally unlabeled). Links referenced: shared benchmark sheet: https://redwood.ai/sheets/fin_qntz_202507, security packet: https://redwood.ai/docs/soc2_finsight.pdf.
